q.t: A shape with ALL its sides equal is called:
q.e: That is what ‘regular’ means for a shape — every side the same length.

q.t: How many squares fit around one point, with no gaps?
q.e: Each square corner is a quarter turn, and 4 quarters make a full turn.

q.t: How many equilateral triangles fit around one point, with no gaps?
q.e: Each corner is a sixth of a full turn, so 6 close up exactly.

q.t: How many regular hexagons fit around one point, with no gaps?
q.e: Each hexagon corner is a third of a full turn, so 3 fill the turn.

q.t: Which regular shape does NOT tessellate (cover a floor with no gaps)?
q.e: 3 pentagons around a point leave a gap, but a 4th is too big to fit.

q.t: A tessellation covers a surface:
o: With no gaps and no overlaps
With shapes on top of each other
q.e: Every bit is covered exactly once — nothing missed, nothing doubled.

q.t: How many squares are in the net of a cube?
q.e: A cube has 6 faces, and each face is one square of the net.

q.t: A shape with four sides is called a:
q.e: ‘Quad’ means four.

q.t: Every point on this shape is the same distance from its centre:
q.e: That is why a compass draws a circle — the pencil keeps the same distance from the point.

q.t: Row 1 of a mat is ‘1 over, 1 under’. What is Row 2?
q.e: Row 2 must be the opposite of Row 1, so the strips hold each other.

q.t: How many sides does a hexagon have?
q.e: ‘Hexa’ means six.

q.t: How many sides does a pentagon have?
q.e: ‘Penta’ means five.

q.t: How many faces does a dodecahedron have?
q.e: ‘Dodeca’ means twelve — the name counts the faces.

q.t: How many faces does an icosahedron have?
q.e: ‘Icosa’ means twenty — the name counts the faces.

q.t: I have 4 equal sides and 4 right angles. What am I?
q.e: A rhombus also has 4 equal sides, but only a square also has 4 right angles.

q.t: I have 4 equal sides, but my corners are NOT right angles. What am I?
q.e: A rhombus is like a square that has been pushed over.

q.t: A quadrilateral with just ONE pair of parallel sides is a:
q.e: The others all have two pairs of parallel sides.

q.t: I have 4 right angles and opposite sides equal, but not all sides equal. What am I?
q.e: A square would need all four sides equal.

q.t: Why is Row 2 of a woven mat the opposite of Row 1?
o: So the strips hold each other and the mat does not fall apart
q.e: If both rows went over in the same places, nothing would trap the strips.

q.t: Can circles cover a table with no gaps?
o: No — small gaps are left between them
q.e: Push circles as close as you like and curved gaps remain.

q.t: Four squares meet at a point. How big is each square’s corner?
q.e: 4 equal corners share a full turn, so each is 1/4 — a right angle.

q.t: Six equilateral triangles meet at a point. How big is each corner?
q.e: 6 equal corners share one full turn.

q.t: Three regular hexagons meet at a point. How big is each corner?
q.e: 3 equal corners share one full turn.

q.t: Why don’t regular pentagons tessellate?
o: 3 leave a gap and a 4th does not fit
q.e: A pentagon’s corner is more than a quarter turn but less than a third, so no whole number of them makes a full turn.

q.t: A square is also a special kind of:
q.e: It has 4 right angles like a rectangle and 4 equal sides like a rhombus.

q.t: I have two pairs of equal sides, and the equal sides are next to each other. What am I?
q.e: In a kite the equal sides meet; in a rectangle or parallelogram they are opposite.

q.t: Row 1 of a mat is ‘2 over, 1 under’. What is Row 2?
q.e: Row 2 is the opposite of Row 1: wherever Row 1 went over, Row 2 goes under.

q.t: Which is TRUE about nets of a cube?
o: Not every arrangement of 6 squares folds into a cube
Any 6 joined squares fold into a cube
q.e: In some arrangements two squares try to land on the same face.

q.t: How many more sides does a regular hexagon have than an equilateral triangle?
q.e: A hexagon has 6 sides and a triangle has 3.

q.t: Two identical equilateral triangles are joined along one side. What shape do they make?
q.e: All 4 outside sides are equal, but the corners are not right angles.

q.t: Around one point you place 2 squares. How many equilateral triangles will fill the rest exactly?
q.e: 2 squares use 2 quarters = half a turn. The other half is 3 sixths, so 3 triangles.

q.t: Around one point you place 1 regular hexagon. How many equilateral triangles fill the rest?
q.e: A hexagon corner is 1/3 = 2/6, leaving 4/6 — four triangle corners.

q.t: Around one point you place 2 regular hexagons. How many equilateral triangles fill the rest?
q.e: 2 hexagons use 2/3 of the turn; the last 1/3 = 2/6 fits 2 triangles.

q.t: In a mat, Row 1 starts ‘over’ and every row is the opposite of the row before. What does Row 6 start with?
q.e: The rows go over, under, over, under, over, under — even rows start ‘under’.

q.t: Row 1 of a mat is ‘2 over, 1 under’, repeated across 12 strips. How many ‘over’s are in Row 1?
q.e: The pattern repeats every 3 strips, so it repeats 4 times, with 2 overs each time.

q.t: How many more faces does an icosahedron have than a dodecahedron?
q.e: Icosa = 20 and dodeca = 12, and 20 − 12 = 8.

q.t: Which clue alone is enough to tell a square from a rhombus?
q.e: Both have four equal sides and parallel sides; only the square has right angles.

q.t: How many sides do 3 regular pentagons and 2 regular hexagons have altogether?
Rahul places 3 regular hexagons around a point and then tries to add a triangle there. What happens?
o: It overlaps — the 3 hexagons already fill the full turn
q.e: 3 thirds already make one full turn, so there is no room left.

q.t: Six squares are joined in one long straight row. Does it fold into a cube?
o: No — some faces land on top of each other
q.e: Folding the row round makes a loop of 4 faces; the last 2 squares cover faces already used, and the top and bottom stay open.
